The solution of this difficulty is: Nebuchadnezzar first ruled as subordinate to his father Nabopolassar, to which time the first chapter refers (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Da 1:1</reference>); whereas "the second year" in the second chapter is dated from his sole sovereignty. The very difficulty is a proof of genuineness; all was clear to the writer and the original readers from their knowledge of the circumstances, and so he adds no explanation. A forger would not introduce difficulties; the author did not then see any difficulty in the case. Nebuchadnezzar is called "king" (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Da 1:1</reference>), by anticipation. Before he left Judea, he became actual king by the death of his father, and the Jews always called him "king," as commander of the invading army.<div eID="gen21571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dreams--</hi>It is significant that not to Daniel, but to the then world ruler, Nebuchadnezzar, the dream is vouchsafed. It was from the first of its representatives who had conquered the theocracy, that the world power was to learn its doom, as about to be in its turn subdued, and for ever by the kingdom of God. As this vision opens, so that in the seventh chapter developing the same truth more fully, closes the first part. Nebuchadnezzar, as vicegerent of God (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jr 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12-Ezek.28.15">Eze 28:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">45:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Ro 13:1</reference>), is honored with the revelation in the form of a dream, the appropriate form to one outside the kingdom of God. So in the cases of Abimelech, Pharaoh, &c. (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.3">Ge 20:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.1-Gen.41.7">41:1-7</reference>), especially as the heathen attached such importance to dreams. Still it is not he, but an Israelite, who interprets it. Heathendom is passive, Israel active, in divine things, so that the glory redounds to "the God of heaven." <div eID="gen21572" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1a4bd34f847337f9b6384232f9648fd94ec3c2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11942"/><div sID="gen21573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11942"/><hi type="bold">2. Chaldeans--</hi>here, a certain order of priest-magicians, who wore a peculiar dress, like that seen on the gods and deified men in the Assyrian sculptures. Probably they belonged exclusively to the Chaldeans, the original tribe of the Babylonian nation, just as the Magians were properly Medes. <div eID="gen21573" type="x-p"/>
entries.c91f7670565f58791fac9955cfb87dca3bd70646: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11943"/><div sID="gen21574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11943"/><hi type="bold">3. troubled to know the dream--</hi>He awoke in alarm, remembering that something solemn had been presented to him in a dream, without being able to recall the form in which it had clothed itself. His thoughts on the unprecedented greatness to which his power had attained (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Da 2:29</reference>) made him anxious to know what the issue of all this should be. God meets this wish in the way most calculated to impress him. <div eID="gen21574" type="x-p"/>
entries.e08dbfc1d4d292f0feeb462436db0b1fc833c18c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11944"/><div sID="gen21575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11944"/>4. Here begins the Chaldee portion of Daniel, which continues to the end of the seventh chapter. In it the course, character, and crisis of the Gentile power are treated; whereas, in the other parts, which are in Hebrew, the things treated apply more particularly to the Jews and Jerusalem.<div eID="gen21575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Syriac--</hi>the Aramean Chaldee, the vernacular tongue of the king and his court; the prophet, by mentioning it here, hints at the reason of his own adoption of it from this point.<div eID="gen21576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live for ever--</hi>a formula in addressing kings, like our "Long live the king!" Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.31">1Ki 1:31</reference>. <div eID="gen21577" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e53a4e20addae9965bdfba369afbc8e0e467ccf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11945"/><div sID="gen21578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11945"/><hi type="bold">5. The thing--</hi>that is, The dream, "is gone from me." Gesenius translates, "The decree is gone forth from me," irrevocable (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Is 45:23</reference>); namely, that you shall be executed, if you do not tell both the dream and the interpretation. English Version is simpler, which supposes the king himself to have forgotten the dream. Pretenders to supernatural knowledge often bring on themselves their own punishment.<div eID="gen21578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut in pieces--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.33">1Sa 15:33</reference>).<div eID="gen21579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">houses ... dunghill--</hi>rather, "a morass heap." The Babylonian houses were built of sun-dried bricks; when demolished, the rain dissolves the whole into a mass of mire, in the wet land, near the river [Stuart]. As to the consistency of this cruel threat with Nebuchadnezzar's character, see <reference osisRef="Dan.4.17">Da 4:17</reference>, "basest of men"; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.5">Jr 39:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9-Jer.52.11">52:9-11</reference>. <div eID="gen21580" type="x-p"/>
entries.204beb2bd2d43e2f4908f42052bbd4441729ab36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11946"/><div sID="gen21581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11946"/><hi type="bold">6. rewards--</hi>literally, "presents poured out in lavish profusion." <div eID="gen21581" type="x-p"/>
entries.88d7208e8be59e98458abc76afd1ee87f6f58905: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11947"/><div sID="gen21582" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11947"/><hi type="bold">8. gain ... time--</hi>literally, "buy." Compare <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">Ep 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>, where the sense is somewhat different.<div eID="gen21582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21583" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the thing is gone from me--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.5">Da 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21583" type="x-p"/>
entries.56a1e195502ba1ae158a91bfe351b9d3270e2a37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11948"/><div sID="gen21584" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11948"/><hi type="bold">9. one decree--</hi>There can be no second one reversing the first (<reference osisRef="Esth.4.11">Es 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen21584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corrupt--</hi>deceitful.<div eID="gen21585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till the time be changed--</hi>till a new state of things arrive, either by my ceasing to trouble myself about the dream, or by a change of government (which perhaps the agitation caused by the dream made Nebuchadnezzar to forebode, and so to suspect the Chaldeans of plotting).<div eID="gen21586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tell ... dream, and I shall know ... ye can show ... interpretation--</hi>If ye cannot tell the past, a dream actually presented to me, how can ye know, and show, the future events prefigured in it? <div eID="gen21587" type="x-p"/>
entries.f970c728d18075c3a666869e31ac10fbda17b337: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11949"/><div sID="gen21588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11949"/><hi type="bold">10. There is not a man ... that can show--</hi>God makes the heathen out of their own mouth, condemn their impotent pretensions to supernatural knowledge, in order to bring out in brighter contrast His power to reveal secrets to His servants, though but "men upon the earth" (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.2.22">Da 2:22</reference>, 23).<div eID="gen21588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore, &c.--</hi>that is, If such things could be done by men, other absolute princes would have required them from their magicians; as they have not, it is proof such things cannot be done and cannot be reasonably asked from us. <div eID="gen21589" type="x-p"/>
entries.cffdca0adc09b4e496428c12333f5b567cb82018: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11950"/><div sID="gen21590" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11950"/><hi type="bold">11. gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh--</hi>answering to "no man upon the earth"; for there were, in their belief, "men in heaven," namely, men deified; for example, Nimrod. The supreme gods are referred to here, who alone, in the Chaldean view, could solve the difficulty, but who do not communicate with men. The inferior gods, intermediate between men and the supreme gods, are unable to solve it. Contrast with this heathen idea of the utter severance of God from man, <reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>, "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us"; Daniel was in this case made His representative. <div eID="gen21590" type="x-p"/>
entries.72eda775ad95ba76477a36b5a35ef36bb3a480b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11951"/><div sID="gen21591" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11951"/>12-13. Daniel and his companions do not seem to have been actually numbered among the Magi or Chaldeans, and so were not summoned before the king. Providence ordered it so that all mere human wisdom should be shown vain before His divine power, through His servant, was put forth. <reference osisRef="Dan.2.24">Da 2:24</reference> shows that the decree for slaying the wise men had not been actually executed when Daniel interposed. <div eID="gen21591" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae81e2e33f350b003bc5e24345e8253225265704: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11952"/><div sID="gen21592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11952"/><hi type="bold">14. captain of the king's guard--</hi>commanding the executioners (Margin; and <reference osisRef="Gen.37.36">Ge 37:36</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen21592" type="x-p"/>
entries.671b00d82e1edd045c0511aedd82eadc1863e558: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11953"/><div sID="gen21593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11953"/><hi type="bold">15. Why is the decree so hasty--</hi>Why were not all of us consulted before the decree for the execution of all was issued?<div eID="gen21593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the thing--</hi>the agitation of the king as to his dream, and his abortive consultation of the Chaldeans. It is plain from this that Daniel was till now ignorant of the whole matter. <div eID="gen21594" type="x-p"/>
entries.d09f47e0e8f09865e12c8b981719c83342f7db7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11954"/><div sID="gen21595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11954"/><hi type="bold">16. Daniel went in--</hi>perhaps not in person, but by the mediation of some courtier who had access to the king. His first direct interview seems to have been <reference osisRef="Dan.2.25">Da 2:25</reference> [Barnes].<div eID="gen21595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">time--</hi>The king granted "time" to Daniel, though he would not do so to the Chaldeans because they betrayed their lying purpose by requiring him to tell the dream, which Daniel did not. Providence doubtless influenced his mind, already favorable (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.19">Da 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>), to show special favor to Daniel. <div eID="gen21596" type="x-p"/>
entries.b892b9ca6ef8175a40a2052a9a80e7117230ce2c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11955"/><div sID="gen21597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11955"/>17. Here appears the reason why Daniel sought "time" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.16">Da 2:16</reference>), namely he wished to engage his friends to join him in prayer to God to reveal the dream to him. <div eID="gen21597" type="x-p"/>
entries.924bea8856d7a0b8934bede79e6ab534c49206a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11956"/><div sID="gen21598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11956"/>18. An illustration of the power of united prayer (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.19">Mt 18:19</reference>). The same instrumentality rescued Peter from his peril (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.5-Acts.12.12">Ac 12:5-12</reference>). <div eID="gen21598" type="x-p"/>
entries.c07ed125c03bfa88174b6d374e5bf8b45ec5b830: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11957"/><div sID="gen21599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11957"/><hi type="bold">19. revealed ... in ... night vision--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.33.15">Job 33:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen21599" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd63af204968ac9e76d315b09db158a30d487940: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11958"/><div sID="gen21600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11958"/><hi type="bold">20. answered--</hi>responded to God's goodness by praises.<div eID="gen21600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name of God--</hi>God in His revelation of Himself by acts of love, "wisdom, and might" (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">Jr 32:19</reference>). <div eID="gen21601" type="x-p"/>
entries.643297d4283de2ddf950341d161458290a40c604: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11959"/><div sID="gen21602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11959"/><hi type="bold">21. changeth ... times ... seasons--</hi>"He herein gives a general preparatory intimation, that the dream of Nebuchadnezzar is concerning the changes and successions of kingdoms" [Jerome]. The "times" are the phases and periods of duration of empires (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.32">1Ch 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.30">29:30</reference>); the "seasons" the fitting times for their culmination, decline, and fall (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.1">Ec 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Ac 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.1">1Th 5:1</reference>). The vicissitudes of states, with their times and seasons, are not regulated by chance or fate, as the heathen thought, but by God.<div eID="gen21602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">removed kings--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.12.18">Job 12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.6">Psa 75:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.5">Jr 27:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.7">1Sa 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen21603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">giveth wisdom--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.9-1Kgs.3.12">1Ki 3:9-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">Jas 1:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21604" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e518920fd596ce0750b7e52dda6ce93416f7f9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11960"/><div sID="gen21605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11960"/><hi type="bold">22. revealeth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.12.22">Job 12:22</reference>). So spiritually (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.17">Ep 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen21605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth what is in ... darkness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.139.11">Psa 139:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.13">He 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen21606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light ... him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.4">1Jo 1:4</reference>). Apocalypse (or "revelation") signifies a divine, prophecy a human, activity. Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.6">1Co 14:6</reference>, where the two are distinguished. The prophet is connected with the outer world, addressing to the congregation the words with which the Spirit of God supplies him; he speaks in the Spirit, but the apocalyptic seer is in the Spirit in his whole person (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.2">4:2</reference>). The form of the apocalyptic revelation (the very term meaning that the veil that hides the invisible world is taken off) is subjectively either the dream, or, higher, the vision. The interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream was a preparatory education to Daniel himself. By gradual steps, each revelation preparing him for the succeeding one, God fitted him for disclosures becoming more and more special. In the second and fourth chapters he is but an interpreter of Nebuchadnezzar's dreams; then he has a dream himself, but it is only a vision in a dream of the night (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.1">Da 7:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.2">2</reference>); then follows a vision in a waking state (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.1-Dan.8.3">Da 8:1-3</reference>); lastly, in the two final revelations (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.20">Da 9:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.4">10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.5">5</reference>) the ecstatic state is no longer needed. The progression in the form answers to the progression in the contents of his prophecy; at first general outlines, and these afterwards filled up with minute chronological and historical details, such as are not found in the Revelation of John, though, as became the New Testament, the form of revelation is the highest, namely, clear waking visions [Auberlen]. <div eID="gen21607" type="x-p"/>
entries.7143975cc3ca9c3857557aa3a6d3168a71c2d6e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11961"/><div sID="gen21608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11961"/><hi type="bold">23. thee ... thee--</hi>He ascribes all the glory to God.<div eID="gen21608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God of my fathers--</hi>Thou hast shown Thyself the same God of grace to me, a captive exile, as Thou didst to Israel of old and this on account of the covenant made with our "fathers" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.54">Lu 1:54</reference>, 55; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>).<div eID="gen21609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given me wisdom and might--</hi>Thou being the fountain of both; referring to <reference osisRef="Dan.2.20">Da 2:20</reference>. Whatever wise ability I have to stay the execution of the king's cruel decree, is Thy gift.<div eID="gen21610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">me ... we ... us--</hi>The revelation was given to Daniel, as "me" implies; yet with just modesty he joins his friends with him; because it was to their joint prayers, and not to his individually, that he owed the revelation from God.<div eID="gen21611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known ... the king's matter--</hi>the very words in which the Chaldeans had denied the possibility of any man on earth telling the dream ("not a man upon the earth can show the king's matter," <reference osisRef="Dan.2.10">Da 2:10</reference>). Impostors are compelled by the God of truth to eat up their own words. <div eID="gen21612" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c08b26312d618d451a2e150d37217f7f5ebf26f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11962"/><div sID="gen21613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11962"/><hi type="bold">24. Therefore--</hi>because of having received the divine communication.<div eID="gen21613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring me in before the king--</hi>implying that he had not previously been in person before the king (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.16">Da 2:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21614" type="x-p"/>
entries.6345ba9ba0f8fd332cde8a1f5b8eaeb354d01e71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11963"/><div sID="gen21615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11963"/><hi type="bold">25. I have found a man--</hi>Like all courtiers, in announcing agreeable tidings, he ascribes the merit of the discovery to himself [Jerome]. So far from it being a discrepancy, that he says nothing of the previous understanding between him and Daniel, or of Daniel's application to the king (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.15">Da 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>), it is just what we should expect. Arioch would not dare to tell an absolute despot that he had stayed the execution of his sanguinary decree, on his own responsibility; but would, in the first instance, secretly stay it until Daniel had got, by application from the king, the time required, without Arioch seeming to know of Daniel's application as the cause of the respite; then, when Daniel had received the revelation, Arioch would in trembling haste bring him in, as if then for the first time he had "found" him. The very difficulty when cleared up is a proof of genuineness, as it never would be introduced by a forger. <div eID="gen21615" type="x-p"/>
entries.08980a05f0c4817c3561fff72cef630f8a659115: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11964"/><div sID="gen21616" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11964"/><hi type="bold">27. cannot--</hi>Daniel, being learned in all the lore of the Chaldeans (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.4">Da 1:4</reference>), could authoritatively declare the impossibility of mere man solving the king's difficulty.<div eID="gen21616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soothsayers--</hi>from a root, "to cut off"; referring to their cutting the heavens into divisions, and so guessing at men's destinies from the place of the stars at one's birth. <div eID="gen21617" type="x-p"/>
entries.a397b6150b1b7c7873c82c929527e17e77d5be08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11965"/><div sID="gen21618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11965"/><hi type="bold">28. God--</hi>in contrast to "the wise men," &c. (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.27">Da 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen21618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revealeth secrets--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.3.7">Am 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">4:13</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Ge 41:45</reference>, Zaphnath-paaneah, "revealer of secrets," the title given to Joseph.<div eID="gen21619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the latter days--</hi>literally, "in the after days" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.29">Da 2:29</reference>); "hereafter" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.1">Ge 49:1</reference>). It refers to the whole future, including the Messianic days, which is the final dispensation (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen21620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visions of thy head--</hi>conceptions formed in the brain. <div eID="gen21621" type="x-p"/>
entries.eea896c3bb101febe1a14dd5516a23293cab7654: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11966"/><div sID="gen21622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11966"/>29. God met with a revelation Nebuchadnezzar, who had been meditating on the future destiny of his vast empire. <div eID="gen21622" type="x-p"/>
entries.53da70c92e571ada0e95ca772fade18eb89e66c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11967"/><div sID="gen21623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11967"/><hi type="bold">30. not ... for any wisdom that I have--</hi>not on account of any previous wisdom which I may have manifested (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.17">Da 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). The specially-favored servants of God in all ages disclaim merit in themselves and ascribe all to the grace and power of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.16">Ge 41:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.12">Ac 3:12</reference>). The "as for me," disclaiming extraordinary merit, contrasts elegantly with "as for thee," whereby Daniel courteously, but without flattery, implies, that God honored Nebuchadnezzar, as His vicegerent over the world kingdoms, with a revelation on the subject uppermost in his thoughts, the ultimate destinies of those kingdoms.<div eID="gen21623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for their sakes that shall make known, &c.--</hi>a Chaldee idiom for, "to the intent that the interpretation may be made known to the king."<div eID="gen21624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the thoughts of thy heart--</hi>thy subject of thought before falling asleep. Or, perhaps the probation of Nebuchadnezzar's character through this revelation may be the meaning intended (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2Ch 32:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.35">Lu 2:35</reference>). <div eID="gen21625" type="x-p"/>
entries.72a9a6f82d88a7717e1ac0feeb629a6caa1385ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11968"/><div sID="gen21626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11968"/>31. The world power in its totality appears as a colossal human form: Babylon the head of gold, Medo-Persia the breast and two arms of silver, Græco-Macedonia the belly and two thighs of brass, and Rome, with its Germano-Slavonic offshoots, the legs of iron and feet of iron and clay, the fourth still existing. Those kingdoms only are mentioned which stand in some relation to the kingdom of God; of these none is left out; the final establishment of that kingdom is the aim of His moral government of the world. The colossus of metal stands on weak feet, of clay. All man's glory is as ephemeral and worthless as chaff (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.24">1Pe 1:24</reference>). But the kingdom of God, small and unheeded as a "stone" on the ground is compact in its homogeneous unity; whereas the world power, in its heterogeneous constituents successively supplanting one another, contains the elements of decay. The relation of the stone to the mountain is that of the kingdom of the cross (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">Mt 16:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.26">Lu 24:26</reference>) to the kingdom of glory, the latter beginning, and the former ending when the kingdom of God breaks in pieces the kingdoms of the world (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>). Christ's contrast between the two kingdoms refers to this passage.<div eID="gen21626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a great image--</hi>literally, "one image that was great." Though the kingdoms were different, it was essentially one and the same world power under different phases, just as the image was one, though the parts were of different metals. <div eID="gen21627" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ae9afc0628d980df18e11e17ad82139e2f062dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11969"/><div sID="gen21628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11969"/>32. On ancient coins states are often represented by human figures. The head and higher parts signify the earlier times; the lower, the later times. The metals become successively baser and baser, implying the growing degeneracy from worse to worse. Hesiod, two hundred years before Daniel, had compared the four ages to the four metals in the same order; the idea is sanctioned here by Holy Writ. It was perhaps one of those fragments of revelation among the heathen derived from the tradition as to the fall of man. The metals lessen in specific gravity, as they downwards; silver is not so heavy as gold, brass not so heavy as silver, and iron not so heavy as brass, the weight thus being arranged in the reverse of stability [Tregelles]. Nebuchadnezzar derived his authority from God, not from man, nor as responsible to man. But the Persian king was so far dependent on others that he could not deliver Daniel from the princes (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.14">Da 6:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.15">15</reference>); contrast <reference osisRef="Dan.5.18">Da 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">19</reference>, as to Nebuchadnezzar's power from God, "whom he would he slew, and whom he would he kept alive" (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.14">Ezr 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.1.13-Esth.1.16">Es 1:13-16</reference>). Græco-Macedonia betrays its deterioration in its divisions, not united as Babylon and Persia. Iron is stronger than brass, but inferior in other respects; so Rome hardy and strong to tread down the nations, but less kingly and showing its chief deterioration in its last state. Each successive kingdom incorporates its predecessor (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.5.28">Da 5:28</reference>). Power that in Nebuchadnezzar's hands was a God-derived (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>, 38) autocracy, in the Persian king's was a rule resting on his nobility of person and birth, the nobles being his equals in rank, but not in office; in Greece, an aristocracy not of birth, but individual influence, in Rome, lowest of all, dependent entirely on popular choice, the emperor being appointed by popular military election. <div eID="gen21628" type="x-p"/>
entries.da3f2ed3d9474ec804af8a3200bdb2f965f87610: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11970"/><div sID="gen21629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11970"/>33. As the two arms of silver denote the kings of the Medes and Persians [Josephus]; and the two thighs of brass the Seleucidæ of Syria and Lagidæ of Egypt, the two leading sections into which Græco-Macedonia parted, so the two legs of iron signify the two Roman consuls [Newton]. The clay, in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.41">Da 2:41</reference>, "potter's clay," <reference osisRef="Dan.2.43">Da 2:43</reference>, "miry clay," means "earthenware," hard but brittle (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.27">Re 2:27</reference>, where the same image is used of the same event); the feet are stable while bearing only direct pressure, but easily broken to pieces by a blow (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>), the iron intermixed not retarding, but hastening, such a result. <div eID="gen21629" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c40fac3cda3cce5eb2cc6e13dfc6a53c36a76d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11971"/><div sID="gen21630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11971"/><hi type="bold">34. stone--</hi>Messiah and His kingdom (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Ge 49:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Is 28:16</reference>). In its relations to Israel, it is a "stone of stumbling" (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Is 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.11">Ac 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>) on which both houses of Israel are broken, not destroyed (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.32">Mt 21:32</reference>). In its relation to the Church, the same stone which destroys the image is the foundation of the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>). In its relation to the Gentile world power, the stone is its destroyer (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Da 2:35</reference>, 44; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.12.3">Zec 12:3</reference>). Christ saith (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mt 21:44</reference>, referring to <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Is 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.15">15</reference>), "Whosoever shall fall on this stone (that is, stumble, and be offended, at Him, as the Jews were, from whom, therefore, He says, 'The kingdom shall be taken') shall be broken; but (referring to <reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 35) on whomsoever it shall fall (referring to the world power which had been the instrument of breaking the Jews), it will (not merely break, but) grind him to powder" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>). The falling of the stone of the feet of the image cannot refer to Christ at His first advent, for the fourth kingdom was not then as yet divided--no toes were in existence (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>).<div eID="gen21630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut out--</hi>namely, from "the mountain" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Da 2:45</reference>); namely, Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>), and antitypically, the heavenly mount of the Father's glory, from whom Christ came.<div eID="gen21631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without hands--</hi>explained in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>, "The God of heaven shall set up a kingdom," as contrasted with the image which was made with hands of man. Messiah not created by human agency, but conceived by the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.20">Mt 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Lu 1:35</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.58">Mr 14:58</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.11">He 9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">24</reference>). So "not made with hands," that is, heavenly, <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>; spiritual, <reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>. The world kingdoms were reared by human ambition: but this is the "kingdom of heaven"; "not of this world" (<reference osisRef="John.18.36">Joh 18:36</reference>). As the fourth kingdom, or Rome, was represented in a twofold state, first strong, with legs of iron, then weak, with toes part of iron, part of clay; so this fifth kingdom, that of Christ, is seen conversely, first insignificant as a "stone," then as a "mountain" filling the whole earth. The ten toes are the ten lesser kingdoms into which the Roman kingdom was finally to be divided; this tenfold division here hinted at is not specified in detail till the seventh chapter. The fourth empire originally was bounded in Europe pretty nearly by the line of the Rhine and Danube; in Asia by the Euphrates. In Africa it possessed Egypt and the north coasts; South Britain and Dacia were afterwards added but were ultimately resigned. The ten kingdoms do not arise until a deterioration (by mixing clay with the iron) has taken place; they are in existence when Christ comes in glory, and then are broken in pieces. The ten have been sought for in the invading hosts of the fifth and sixth century. But though many provinces were then severed from Rome as independent kingdoms, the dignity of emperor still continued, and the imperial power was exercised over Rome itself for two centuries. So the tenfold divisions cannot be looked for before A.D. 731. But the East is not to be excluded, five toes being on each foot. Thus no point of time before the overthrow of the empire at the taking of Constantinople by the Turks (A.D. 1453) can be assigned for the division. It seems, therefore, that the definite ten will be the ultimate development of the Roman empire just before the rise of Antichrist, who shall overthrow three of the kings, and, after three and a half years, he himself be overthrown by Christ in person. Some of the ten kingdoms will, doubtless, be the same as some past and present divisions of the old Roman empire, which accounts for the continuity of the connection between the toes and legs, a gap of centuries not being interposed, as is objected by opponents of the futurist theory. The lists of the ten made by the latter differ from one another; and they are set aside by the fact that they include countries which were never Roman, and exclude one whole section of the empire, namely, the East [Tregelles].<div eID="gen21632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon his feet--</hi>the last state of the Roman empire. Not "upon his legs." Compare "in the days of these kings" (see on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>). <div eID="gen21633" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ac026377e00859301159ba6d108081d48a33218: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11972"/><div sID="gen21634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11972"/><hi type="bold">35. broken ... together--</hi>excluding a contemporaneous existence of the kingdom of the world and the kingdom of God (in its manifested, as distinguished from its spiritual, phase). The latter is not gradually to wear away the former, but to destroy it at once, and utterly (2Th 1:7-10; 2:8). However, the Hebrew may be translated, "in one discriminate mass."<div eID="gen21634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chaff--</hi>image of the ungodly, as they shall be dealt with in the judgment (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.4">Psa 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>).<div eID="gen21635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21636" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">summer threshing-floors--</hi>Grain was winnowed in the East on an elevated space in the open air, by throwing the grain into the air with a shovel, so that the wind might clear away the chaff.<div eID="gen21636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no place ... found for them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rev.20.11">Re 20:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.10">Psa 37:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">103:16</reference>).<div eID="gen21637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">became ... mountain--</hi>cut out of the mountain (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Da 2:45</reference>) originally, it ends in becoming a mountain. So the kingdom of God, coming from heaven originally, ends in heaven being established on earth (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.1-Rev.21.3">Re 21:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen21638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filled ... earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>). It is to do so in connection with Jerusalem as the mother Church (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.9">Psa 80:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>). <div eID="gen21639" type="x-p"/>
entries.af4c1c26eb021a6f8b925695956b1f2479f70c25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11973"/><div sID="gen21640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11973"/><hi type="bold">36. we--</hi>Daniel and his three friends. <div eID="gen21640" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e9cacbedd58cf536e00e5dd56b2ea420a67ddcc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11974"/><div sID="gen21641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11974"/><hi type="bold">37. Thou ... art a king of kings--</hi>The committal of power in fullest plenitude belongs to Nebuchadnezzar personally, as having made Babylon the mighty empire it was. In twenty-three years after him the empire was ended: with him its greatness is identified (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Da 4:30</reference>), his successors having done nothing notable. Not that he actually ruled every part of the globe, but that God granted him illimitable dominion in whatever direction his ambition led him, Egypt, Nineveh, Arabia, Syria, Tyre, and its Phoenician colonies (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.5-Jer.27.8">Jr 27:5-8</reference>). Compare as to Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.2">Ezr 1:2</reference>. <div eID="gen21641" type="x-p"/>
entries.5001def173efc0581130bd57b35eda0607587da9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11975"/><div sID="gen21642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11975"/><hi type="bold">38. men ... beasts ... fowls--</hi>the dominion originally designed for man (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.28">Ge 1:28</reference>; 2:19, 20), forfeited by sin; temporarily delegated to Nebuchadnezzar and the world powers; but, as they abuse the trust for self, instead of for God, to be taken from them by the Son of man, who will exercise it for God, restoring in His person to man the lost inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6">Psa 8:4-6</reference>).<div eID="gen21642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou art ... head of gold--</hi>alluding to the riches of Babylon, hence called "the golden city" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.7">Jr 51:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.16">Re 18:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21643" type="x-p"/>
entries.068a965e77ed5d7f4e9816fb4f4f647937c86ffd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11976"/><div sID="gen21644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11976"/>39. That Medo-Persia is the second kingdom appears from <reference osisRef="Dan.5.28">Da 5:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.8.20">Da 8:20</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.20">2Ch 36:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Is 21:2</reference>.<div eID="gen21644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21645" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inferior--</hi>"The kings of Persia were the worst race of men that ever governed an empire" [Prideaux]. Politically (which is the main point of view here) the power of the central government in which the nobles shared with the king, being weakened by the growing independence of the provinces, was inferior to that of Nebuchadnezzar, whose sole word was law throughout his empire.<div eID="gen21645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21646" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brass--</hi>The Greeks (the third empire, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.21">Da 8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.20">10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.2-Dan.11.4">11:2-4</reference>) were celebrated for the brazen armor of their warriors. Jerome fancifully thinks that the brass, as being a clear-sounding metal, refers to the eloquence for which Greece was famed. The "belly," in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.32">Da 2:32</reference>, may refer to the drunkenness of Alexander and the luxury of the Ptolemies [Tirinus].<div eID="gen21646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21647" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over all the earth--</hi>Alexander commanded that he should be called "king of all the world" [Justin, 12. sec. 16.9; Arrian, Campaigns of Alexander, 7. sec. 15]. The four successors (diadochi) who divided Alexander's dominions at his death, of whom the Seleucidæ in Syria and the Lagidæ in Egypt were chief, held the same empire. <div eID="gen21647" type="x-p"/>
entries.a64a22d38df92fb2af6529def39f5c22da8b100b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11977"/><div sID="gen21648" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11977"/><hi type="bold">40. iron--</hi>This vision sets forth the character of the Roman power, rather than its territorial extent [Tregelles].<div eID="gen21648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21649" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breaketh in pieces--</hi>So, in righteous retribution, itself will at last be broken in pieces (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>) by the kingdom of God (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Re 13:10</reference>). <div eID="gen21649" type="x-p"/>
entries.0de99ff9a1300bb0aa721e15fbbda1122077f196: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11978"/><div sID="gen21650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11978"/><hi type="bold">41-43. feet ... toes ... part ... clay ... iron--</hi>explained presently, "the kingdom shall be partly strong, partly broken" (rather, "brittle," as earthenware); and <reference osisRef="Dan.2.43">Da 2:43</reference>, "they shall mingle ... with the seed of men," that is, there will be power (in its deteriorated form, iron) mixed up with that which is wholly of man, and therefore brittle; power in the hands of the people having no internal stability, though something is left of the strength of the iron [Tregelles]. Newton, who understands the Roman empire to be parted into the ten kingdoms already (whereas Tregelles makes them future), explains the "clay" mixture as the blending of barbarous nations with Rome by intermarriages and alliances, in which there was no stable amalgamation, though the ten kingdoms retained much of Rome's strength. The "mingling with the seed of men" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>) seems to refer to <reference osisRef="Gen.6.2">Ge 6:2</reference>, where the marriages of the seed of godly Seth with the daughters of ungodly Cain are described in similar words. The reference, therefore, seems to be to the blending of the Christianized Roman empire with the pagan nations, a deterioration being the result. Efforts have been often made to reunite the parts into one great empire, as by Charlemagne and Napoleon, but in vain. Christ alone shall effect that. <div eID="gen21650" type="x-p"/>
entries.89c5512303465628d96e7263404b32d8275f3b25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11979"/><div sID="gen21651" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11979"/><hi type="bold">44. in the days of these kings--</hi>in the days of these kingdoms, that is, of the last of the four. So Christianity was set up when Rome had become mistress of Judea and the world (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Lu 2:1</reference>, &c.) [Newton]. Rather, "in the days of these kings," answers to "upon his feet" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>); that is, the ten toes (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.42">Da 2:42</reference>), or ten kings, the final state of the Roman empire. For "these kings" cannot mean the four successional monarchies, as they do not coexist as the holders of power; if the fourth had been meant, the singular, not the plural, would be used. The falling of the stone on the image must mean, destroying judgment on the fourth Gentile power, not gradual evangelization of it by grace; and the destroying judgment cannot be dealt by Christians, for they are taught to submit to the powers that be, so that it must be dealt by Christ Himself at His coming again. We live under the divisions of the Roman empire which began fourteen hundred years ago, and which at the time of His coming shall be definitely ten. All that had failed in the hand of man shall then pass away, and that which is kept in His own hand shall be introduced. Thus the second chapter is the alphabet of the subsequent prophetic statements in Daniel [Tregelles].<div eID="gen21651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God of heaven ... kingdom--</hi>hence the phrase, "the kingdom of heaven" (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.2">Mt 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen21652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not ... left to other people--</hi>as the Chaldees had been forced to leave their kingdom to the Medo-Persians, and these to the Greeks, and these to the Romans (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.7">Mi 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33).<div eID="gen21653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break ... all--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.60.12">Is 60:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1Co 15:24</reference>). <div eID="gen21654" type="x-p"/>
entries.e208f7649f3d4636e966362ba455ae7bf05d3c6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11980"/><div sID="gen21655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11980"/><hi type="bold">45. without hands--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.35">Da 2:35</reference>). The connection of the "forasmuch," &c. is, "as thou sawest that the stone," &c., this is an indication that "the great God," &c., that is, the fact of thy seeing the dreams as I have recalled it to thy recollection, is a proof that it is no airy phantom, but a real representation to these from God of the future. A similar proof of the "certainty" of the event was given to Pharaoh by the doubling of his dream (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Ge 41:32</reference>). <div eID="gen21655" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1b891bed965fdbe001dee20026e695542af5d1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11981"/><div sID="gen21656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11981"/><hi type="bold">46. fell upon ... face, and worshipped Daniel--</hi>worshipping God in the person of Daniel. Symbolical of the future prostration of the world power before Messiah and His kingdom (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>). As other servants of God refused such honors (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.25">Ac 10:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.13-Acts.14.15">14:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.8">Re 22:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.9">9</reference>), and Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.1.8">Da 1:8</reference>) would not taste defiled food, nor give up prayer to God at the cost of his life (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Da 6:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">10</reference>), it seems likely that Daniel rejected the proffered divine honors. The word "answered" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Da 2:47</reference>) implies that Daniel had objected to these honors; and in compliance with his objection, "the king answered, Of a truth, your God is a God of gods." Daniel had disclaimed all personal merit in <reference osisRef="Dan.2.30">Da 2:30</reference>, giving God all the glory (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.2.45">Da 2:45</reference>).<div eID="gen21656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded ... sweet odours--</hi>divine honors (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.10">Ezr 6:10</reference>). It is not said his command was executed. <div eID="gen21657" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf9d24eee27c81f47231255cf3fca863a700c5d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11982"/><div sID="gen21658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11982"/><hi type="bold">47. Lord of kings--</hi>The world power shall at last have to acknowledge this (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.14">Re 17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.16">19:16</reference>); even as Nebuchadnezzar, who had been the God-appointed "king of kings" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>), but who had abused the trust, is constrained by God's servant to acknowledge that God is the true "Lord of kings." <div eID="gen21658" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d94c746c60185f6a18350a19fa4d2c372ffd582: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11983"/><div sID="gen21659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11983"/>48. One reason for Nebuchadnezzar having been vouchsafed such a dream is here seen; namely, that Daniel might be promoted, and the captive people of God be comforted: the independent state of the captives during the exile and the alleviation of its hardships, were much due to Daniel. <div eID="gen21659" type="x-p"/>
entries.31a406d8a1e820870f5aea1f3413d34a2b2750de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11984"/><div sID="gen21660" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11984"/><hi type="bold">49. Daniel requested--</hi>Contrast this honorable remembrance of his humble friends in his elevation with the spirit of the children of the world in the chief butler's case (<reference osisRef="Gen.40.23">Ge 40:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.15">Ec 9:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Am 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen21660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21661" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the gate--</hi>the place of holding courts of justice and levees in the East (<reference osisRef="Esth.2.19">Es 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>). So "the Sublime Porte," or "Gate," denotes the sultan's government, his counsels being formerly held in the entrance of his palace. Daniel was a chief counsellor of the king, and president over the governors of the different orders into which the Magi were divided. <chapter eID="Dan.2"/>

entries.83a548945289d7e9cf7ff3f9e2666e844f9d8d6c: <div eID="gen32750" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32752" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32751" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32753" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar, in the second year of his reign, (or in the fourth, according to the Jewish account, which takes in the first two years in which he reigned conjointly with his father), had a dream which greatly troubled him; but of which nothing remained in the morning but the uneasy impression. Hence the diviners, when brought in before the king, could give no interpretation, as they were not in possession of the dream, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.1-Dan.2.13">Dan 2:1-13</reference>. Daniel then, having obtained favor from God, is made acquainted with the dream, and its interpretation, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.14-Dan.2.19">Dan 2:14-19</reference>; for which he blesses God in a lofty and beautiful ode, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.20-Dan.2.23">Dan 2:20-23</reference>; and reveals both unto the king, telling him first the particulars of the dream, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.24-Dan.2.35">Dan 2:24-35</reference>, and then interpreting it of the four great monarchies. The then existing Chaldean empire, represented by the head of gold, is the first; the next is the Medo-Persian; the third, the Macedonian or Grecian; the fourth, the Roman, which should break every other kingdom in pieces, but which in its last stage, should be divided into ten kingdoms, represented by the ten toes of the image, as they are in another vision (Daniel 7) by the ten horns of the fourth beast. He likewise informs the king that in the time of this last monarchy, viz., the Roman, God would set up the kingdom of the Messiah; which, though small in its commencement, should ultimately be extended over the whole earth, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.36-Dan.2.45">Dan 2:36-45</reference>. Daniel and his three friends, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, (named by the prince of the eunuchs, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego), are then promoted by the king to great honor, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.46-Dan.2.49">Dan 2:46-49</reference>. <div eID="gen32753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32754" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32755" type="x-p"/> The second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar - That is, the second year of his reigning alone, for he was king two years before his father's death. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan 1:1</reference> (note). This was therefore the fifth year of his reign, and the fourth of the captivity of Daniel. <div eID="gen32755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32756" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams wherewith his spirit was troubled - The dream had made a deep and solemn impression upon his mind; and, having forgotten all but general circumstances, his mind was distressed.
entries.9981b8f646fd5a6ce762367603dd744e38dd9e6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32757" type="x-p"/> The magicians - חרטמים chartummim. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.8">Gen 41:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen32757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32758" type="x-p"/> The astrologers - אשפים ashshaphim. Perhaps from נשף nashaph, to breathe, because they laid claim to Divine inspiration; but probably the persons in question were the philosophers and astronomers among the Babylonians. <div eID="gen32758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32759" type="x-p"/> The sorcerers - מכשפים mechashshephim. See the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.18.10">Deu 18:10</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Exo.22.18">Exo 22:18</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference> (note), where several of these arts are explained. <div eID="gen32759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32760" type="x-p"/> The Chaldeans - Who these were is difficult to be ascertained. They might be a college of learned men, where all arts and sciences were professed and taught. The Chaldeans were the most ancient philosophers of the world; they might have been originally inhabitants of the Babylonian Irak; and still have preserved to themselves exclusively the name of Chaldeans, to distinguish themselves from other nations and peoples who inhabited the one hundred and twenty provinces of which the Babylonish government was composed.
entries.0a63978dba6b660958fb9d9ccf55fbdd67b1500c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32761" type="x-p"/> Then spake the Chaldeans to the king in Syriac - ארמית aramith, the language of Aram or Syria. What has been generally called the Chaldee. <div eID="gen32761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32762" type="x-p"/> O king, live for ever - מלכא לעלמין חיי Malca leolmin cheyi. With these words the Chaldee part of Daniel commences; and continues to the end of the seventh chapter. These kinds of compliments are still in use in the East Indies. A superior gives a blessing to an inferior by saying to him, when the latter is in the act of doing him reverence, "Long life to thee." A poor man, going into the presence of a king to solicit a favor, uses the same kind of address: O father, thou art the support of the destitute; mayest thou live to old age! - Ward's Customs.
entries.84f190694322f3deaa644b4f84939f1e774e8fde: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32763" type="x-p"/> Ye shall be cut in pieces - This was arbitrary and tyrannical in the extreme; but, in the order of God's providence, it was overruled to serve the most important purpose.
entries.98fc1ee631a92dcdffdf86a11edd5d81b7b64770: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32764" type="x-p"/> That ye would gain the time - The king means either that they wished to prolong the time that he might recollect it, or get indifferent about it; or that they might invent something in the place of it; or make their escape to save their lives, after having packed up their valuables. See <reference osisRef="Dan.2.9">Dan 2:9</reference>.
entries.7b56c347c6b0e1b7cf5769704da1277c164ea832: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32765" type="x-p"/> There is not a man upon the earth - The thing is utterly impossible to man. This was their decision: and when Daniel gave the dream, with its interpretation, they knew that the spirit of the holy gods was in him. So, even according to their own theology, he was immeasurably greater than the wisest in Babylon or in the world.
entries.b8f6135d989524ce41d642c554ab95d8d2d0019b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32766" type="x-p"/> They sought Daniel and his fellows - As the decree stated that all the wise men of Babylon should be slain, the four young Hebrews, being reputed among the wisest, were considered as sentenced to death also.
entries.dd02e00cc87757469fae0a278d120217c11e89ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32767" type="x-p"/> Captain of the king's guard - Chief of the king's executioners or slaughter men. Margin, רב תבחיא rab tabachaiya, chief of the butchers, he that took off the heads of those whom the king ordered to be slain, because they had in any case displeased him. "Go and bring me the head of Giaffer." The honorable butcher went and brought the head in a bag on a dish. It was Herod's chief butcher that brought the head of John the Baptist in a dish to the delicate daughter of Herodias. This was the custom of the country. No law, no judge, no jury. The will or caprice of the king governed all things. Happy England! know and value thy excellent privileges!
entries.5ac0a97cb5c174ab002570393896f8f2aec678e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32768" type="x-p"/> That he would give him time - That is, that he might seek unto God for a revelation of the thing. The Chaldeans dared not even to promise this; they would only pledge themselves for the interpretation, provided the king would furnish the dream. Daniel engages both to find the lost dream, and to give the proper interpretation.
entries.6db3c5173c9dd20f6dc07ff20e006de6c9c88e21: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32769" type="x-p"/> That they would desire mercies - For this Daniel had requested a little time; and doubtless both he and his three companions prayed incessantly till God gave the wished for revelation; but whether it was given that same sight, we do not know.
entries.a10bb791fa673af1505823b810e50e548d4e72d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32770" type="x-p"/> Then was the secret revealed - in a night vision - Daniel either dreamed it, or it was represented to his mind by an immediate inspiration.
entries.9e403139394b210510f01373b37a6bd5dccc5c9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32771" type="x-p"/> Wisdom and might are his - He knows all things, and can do all things.
entries.0cffc6c5efda8aa0c83b8122ae96adaff31c7c98: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32772" type="x-p"/> He changeth the times - Time, duration, succession are his, and under his dominion. It is in the course of his providence that one king is put down, and another raised up; and therefore he can distinctly tell what he has purposed to do in the great empires of the earth.
entries.e86521ccf0e5b7809a04c566ee0ee9fff1c77d24: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32773" type="x-p"/> I thank thee and praise thee - No wonder he should feel gratitude, when God by this merciful interference had saved both the life of him and his fellows; and was about to reflect the highest credit on the God of the Jews, and on the people themselves.
entries.4cf47a1739348abcdf8b8f1b004f0200477ab149: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen32773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32774" type="x-p"/> Destroy not the wise men - The decree was suspended till it should be seen whether Daniel could tell the dream, and give its interpretation.
entries.e16e3cd8633087db37ed6f7562e2284b77c769f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen32774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32775" type="x-p"/> Cannot the wise men - Cannot your own able men, aided by your gods, tell you the secret? This question was necessary in order that the king might see the foolishness of depending on the one, or worshipping the other. <div eID="gen32775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32776" type="x-p"/> The soothsayers - One of our old words: "The tellers of truth:" but גזרין gazerin is the name of another class of those curious artists, unless we suppose it to mean the same as the Chaldeans, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.2">Dan 2:2</reference>. They are supposed to be persons who divined by numbers, amulets, etc. There are many conjectures about them, which, whatever learning they show, cast little light upon this place.
entries.c1bdac3f69dfccdc797e8cfb5a52c2f91eb0499b: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen32776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32777" type="x-p"/> There is a God in heaven - To distinguish him from those idols, the works of men's hands; and from the false gods in which the Chaldeans trusted. <div eID="gen32777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32778" type="x-p"/> In the latter days - A phrase which, in the prophets, generally means the times of the Messiah. God is about to show what shall take place from this time to the latest ages of the world. And the vision most certainly contains a very extensive and consecutive prophecy; which I shall treat more largely at the close of the chapter, giving in the mean time a short exposition.
entries.133c518e8af7f62b4059e9a41a77b151309f6156: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen32778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32779" type="x-p"/> A great image - Representing the four great monarchies.
entries.02f4f8c12d397ea8c5057618a3bd130bc5f315f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen32779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32780" type="x-p"/> Head was of fine gold - The Babylonish empire, the first and greatest. <div eID="gen32780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32781" type="x-p"/> Breast and his arms of silver - The Medo-Persian empire, under Cyrus, etc. <div eID="gen32781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32782" type="x-p"/> His belly and his thighs of brass - The Macedonian empire, under Alexander the Great, and his successors.
entries.562d77c3d9efafd41a820d909f93c2312e474a41: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen32782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32783" type="x-p"/> His legs of iron - The Roman government. <div eID="gen32783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32784" type="x-p"/> His feet part of iron and part of clay - The same, mixed with the barbaric nations, and divided into ten kingdoms. See at the end of the chapter.
entries.643477747d037af8e7f5b67bf39f03a1b740f3de: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen32784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32785" type="x-p"/> A stone was cut out - The fifth monarchy; the spiritual kingdom of the Lord Jesus, which is to last for ever, and diffuse itself over the whole earth.
entries.03e31d73dc85565e3e81741fa3a2ea5e7a09d516: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen32785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32786" type="x-p"/> The stone - became a great mountain - There is the kingdom אבן eben, of the stone, and the kingdom of the mountain. See at the end at the chapter.
entries.f23fcf97ada0dfd94a517d1cfb2f9a62ec339657: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen32786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32787" type="x-p"/> The God of heaven - Not given by thy own gods, nor acquired by thy own skill and prowess; it is a Divine gift. <div eID="gen32787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32788" type="x-p"/> Power - To rule this kingdom. <div eID="gen32788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32789" type="x-p"/> And strength - To defend it against all foes. <div eID="gen32789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32790" type="x-p"/> And glory - Great honor and dignity.
entries.ddb92d1f887d94a9efc95d55e627001565aa52d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen32790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32791" type="x-p"/> Thou art this head of gold - See on <reference osisRef="Dan.2.31-Dan.2.34">Dan 2:31-34</reference> (note), and at the end.
entries.31e971b07524d203380371ecfd7e007439faf1a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen32791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32792" type="x-p"/> A kingdom which shall never be destroyed - The extensive and extending empire of Christ. <div eID="gen32792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32793" type="x-p"/> Shall not be left to other people - All the preceding empires have swallowed up each other successively; but this shall remain to the end of the world.
entries.4d33f44e8c3ff901ac5ca0ef16f4d108d90be940: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen32793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32794" type="x-p"/> The dream is certain - It contains a just representation of things as they shall be. <div eID="gen32794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32795" type="x-p"/> And the interpretation thereof sure - The parts of the dream being truly explained. <div eID="gen32795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32796" type="x-p"/> A Discourse on Nebuchadnezzar's Dream <reference osisRef="Dan.2.41-Dan.2.45">Dan 2:41-45</reference> <div eID="gen32796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32797" type="x-p"/> I shall now consider this most important vision more at large, and connect it with a portion of the previous history of the Jewish people. <div eID="gen32797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32798" type="x-p"/> The kingdoms of Israel and Judah after a series of the most unparalleled ingratitude and rebellion, against displays of mercy and benevolence, only equaled by their rebellions, were at last, according to repeated threatenings, given over into the hands of their enemies. The inhabitants of the former country were subdued and carried away captives by the Assyrians; and those of the latter, by the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen32798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32799" type="x-p"/> The people of Israel never recovered their ancient territories; and were so disposed of by their conquerors, that they either became amalgamated with the heathen nations, so as to be utterly undistinguishable; or they were transported to some foreign and recluse place of settlement, that the land of their residence, though repeatedly sought for and guessed at, has for more than two thousand years been totally unknown. <div eID="gen32799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32800" type="x-p"/> Judah, after having been harassed by the Chaldeans, Egyptians, and others, was at last invaded by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon; Jerusalem besieged and taken; and Jehoiachin the king, who had before become tributary to the Babylonians, with his mother, wives, officers of state, and chief military commanders, princes, and mighty men of valor, to the amount of ten thousand; and all the artificers, smiths, etc., to the number of one thousand, with all that were fit for war, he carried captives to Babylon; leaving only the poorest of the people behind, under the government of Mattaniah, son of the late king Josiah, and uncle to Jehoiachin; and, having changed his name to Zedekiah, gave him a nominal authority as king over the wretched remains of the people. Zedekiah, after having reigned nine years, rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, who, coming against Jerusalem with all his forces, besieged it; and having reduced it to the last extremity by famine, and made a breach in the walls, took the city, pillaged and destroyed the temple by fire, slew the sons of Zedekiah before his face, then put out his eyes, and carried him bound in brazen fetters to Babylon, 2 Kings, chap. 24 and 25. Thus, the temple of God, the most glorious building ever laid on the face of the earth, was profaned, pillaged, and burnt, with the king's palace, and all the houses of the Jewish nobility, in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, - the nineteenth of Nebuchadnezzar, - the first of the forty-eight Olympiad, - the one hundred and sixtieth current year of the era of Nabonassar, - four hundred and twenty-four years, three months, and eight days from the time in which Solomon laid its foundation stone! <div eID="gen32800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32801" type="x-p"/> In the same month in which the city was taken, and the temple burnt, Nebuzar-adan, commander in chief of the Babylonish forces, carried off the spoils of the temple, with the Jewish treasures, and the principal part of the residue of the people; and brought them also to Babylon. And thus Judah was carried away out of her own land, four hundred and sixty-eight years after David began to reign over it; from the division under Rehoboam, three hundred and eighty-eight years; from the destruction of the kingdom of Israel, one hundred and thirty-four years; in the year of the world, three thousand four hundred and sixteen; and before the nativity of our Lord, five hundred and eighty-eight. <div eID="gen32801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32802" type="x-p"/> In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, A.M. 3397, b.c. 607, Nebuchadnezzar, having besieged Jerusalem, and made its king tributary, carried away a number of captives; and among them was the Prophet Daniel, then in his youth, who became, for his wisdom, and knowledge of future events, very eminent at Babylon; and, with some other Jewish captives, great favorites of Nebuchadnezzar the king; who made Daniel president of all the wise men of his city. It was in the second year of the reign of this king, that a circumstance occurred which, though at first it threatened the destruction of the prophet, finally issued in the increase of his reputation and celebrity. <div eID="gen32802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32803" type="x-p"/> As prophecy is one of the strongest proofs of the authenticity of what professes to be a Divine revelation, God endued this man with a large portion of his Spirit, so that he clearly predicted some of the most astonishing political occurrences and changes which have ever taken place on the earth; no less than the rise, distinguishing characteristics, and termination of the Four great monarchies or empires, which have been so celebrated in all the histories of the world. And as the Babylonian, under which he then lived, was one of these monarchies, and was shortly to be absorbed by the Medo-Persian, which was to succeed it, he made Nebuchadnezzar, the then reigning monarch, by means of a most singular dream, the particulars of which he had forgotten, the instrument that appeared to give birth to a prediction, in which the ruin of his own empire was foretold; as well as other mighty changes which should take place in the political state of the world, for at least the term of one thousand years next ensuing. Nor did the prophetic Spirit in this eminent man limit his predictions to these; but showed at the same time the origin and nature of that Fifth monarchy, which, under the great King of kings, should be administered and prevail to the end of time. <div eID="gen32803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32804" type="x-p"/> The dream itself, with its interpretation, and the exact and impressive manner in which the predictions relative to the four great monarchies have been fulfilled, and those which regard the fifth monarchy are in the course of being accomplished, are the subjects to which I wish to call the reader's most serious and deliberate attention. <div eID="gen32804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32805" type="x-p"/> This image, so circumstantially described from the thirty-eighth to the forty-fourth verse, was, as we learn from the prophet's general solution, intended to point out the rise and fall of four different empires and states; and the final prevalence and establishment of a fifth empire, that shall never have an end, and which shall commence in the last days, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.28">Dan 2:28</reference>; a phrase commonly used in the prophets to signify the times of the Messiah, and in the New Testament, his advent to judge the world. <div eID="gen32805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32806" type="x-p"/> Before we proceed to particular parts, we may remark in general, that the whole account strongly indicates: - <div eID="gen32806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32807" type="x-p"/> 1. The especial providence of God in behalf of the Jews at that time. For, although suffering grievously because of their sins, being deprived of both their political and personal liberty, God shows them that he has not abandoned them; and the existence of a prophet among them is a proof of his fatherly care and unremitted attention to their eternal welfare. <div eID="gen32807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32808" type="x-p"/> 2. The particular interference of God to manifest the superiority of his truth, to wean an idolatrous nation from their vanity and superstition, and lead them to that God who is the fountain of truth, the revealer of secrets, and the governor of all things. And, <div eID="gen32808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32809" type="x-p"/> 3. The direct inspiration of God immediately teaching his servant things which could be known only to God himself, and thus showing the Babylonians that his prophets had spoken by an unerring Spirit; that the Jews were the depositaries of the true religion; that He was the only true God; and as he was omniscient, so he was omnipotent; and the things which his wisdom had predicted, his power could and would accomplish. <div eID="gen32809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32810" type="x-p"/> The sum of the account given in this chapter is the following: - <div eID="gen32810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32811" type="x-p"/> 1. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in the second year of his reign, about A.M. 3401, and b.c. 603, had a remarkable dream, which, although it made a deep impression on his mind, yet, on his awakening, he found it impossible to recollect; the general impression only remaining. <div eID="gen32811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32812" type="x-p"/> 2. He summoned his wise men, astrologers, etc., told them that he had a dream or vision, which he had forgotten; and commanded them to tell him the dream, and give its interpretation. <div eID="gen32812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32813" type="x-p"/> 3. They request the king to tell them the dream; and promise, then, to make known the meaning. This he could not do, having forgotten it; yet he insists on their compliance on pain of death. <div eID="gen32813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32814" type="x-p"/> 4. To tell the king his dream they find impossible; and a decree for the destruction of the wise men of Babylon is issued, in which Daniel and his fellows are included. <div eID="gen32814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32815" type="x-p"/> 5. Daniel, hearing of it, speaks to Arioch, captain of the king's guard or the royal executioner; desires to be brought before the king; and promises to tell the dream, etc. <div eID="gen32815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32816" type="x-p"/> 6. He is introduced; and immediately tells the king what he had dreamed, and shows him its interpretation. <div eID="gen32816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32817" type="x-p"/> The Dream <div eID="gen32817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32818" type="x-p"/> A vast image, exceedingly luminous, of terrible form, and composed of different substances, appears in a night vision to the king, of which the following is the description: - <div eID="gen32818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32819" type="x-p"/> I. Its head was of fine gold. <div eID="gen32819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32820" type="x-p"/> II. Its breast and arms of silver. <div eID="gen32820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32821" type="x-p"/> III. Its belly and thighs of brass. <div eID="gen32821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32822" type="x-p"/> IV. Its legs of iron, and its feet and toes of iron and clay. While gazing on this image he sees: - <div eID="gen32822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32823" type="x-p"/> V. A stone cut out of a mountain without hands, which smites the image on its feet, and dashes it all to pieces; and the gold, and silver, brass, iron, and clay become as small and as light as chaff. <div eID="gen32823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32824" type="x-p"/> VI.
