                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> gain the time <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This ye do in policy, to escape punishment when taken up with other affairs, I may forget to make further enquiry af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter this thing, but it shall not serve your turn.</ns0:note>, because ye see the thing is gone from me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But if ye will not make known unto me the dream, <ns0:hi>there is but</ns0:hi> one decree for you <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">That is, I will not retract my sentence, ye shall surely dyes you are upon tricks, ye have prepared corrupt and lying words, for he that can interpret a dream can tell the dream, both come from a divine inspiration, which ye pretend to, but, I say, ye have it not.</ns0:note>: for ye have prepared lying and corrupt words to speak before me, till the time be changed: there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore tell me the dream, and I shall know that ye can shew me the interpretation thereof.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:132" />10 ¶ The Chaldeans answered before the king and said, There is not a man upon the earth that can shew the kings matter; therefore <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no king, lord, nor ruler, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> asked such things at any magician, or astrologer, or Chaldean.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 And <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> a rare thing that the king requi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />reth, and there is none other that can shew it before the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> bring three arguments to convince the King. 1. There is not a man upon Earth can shew the Kings matter. 2. There is no King requires such a thing of any Magician. 3. None but the gods can do this. The <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> with other <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> did believe more gods then one, and the supream Deity or Deities did not meddle with the affairs of men, but had the cognisance by inferiour or intermediate <ns0:hi>Demons.</ns0:hi> So <ns0:hi>Plato</ns0:hi> and many of them held, the meaning then is this, seeing there are some things that God who knoweth all things will not commu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nicate the knowledge of to men, and hath not done it to us, it is therefore a singular and unreasonable thing the King should require it of us, and that so suddenly, and upon such penalties.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For this cause the king was angry, and very furious, and commanded to destroy all the wise <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> of Babylon <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Tyrants are inexorable, and they rule according to their will, and being crost they are furious, and that brings forth death, the wrath of such is the <ns0:hi>roaring of a Lion.</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="19">19 ¶ Then was the secret revealed unto Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />niel in a night-vision <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">It is not improbably conjectured that <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> spent the night in Watching and Prayer, for night Vision is distinguished from dreams, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 12.6. whether sleeping or waking <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> had the same thing revealed unto him, which King <ns0:hi>Nebuchad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nezzar</ns0:hi> had, with this difference, the King remembred not his dream nor knew what it meant, but <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> was able to tell his dream and give the meaning of it also.</ns0:note>; Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He gave thanks and praise to the Father of lights, from whom all wisdom comes, who heard his Prayer, and revealed this secret to him.                      </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> he removeth kings and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 12<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> He revealeth the deep and secret things <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Both of nature, wherein are infinite depths, and secrets and of mens Hearts and Counsels which are very close, deep and secret, saying in themselves who can see us, and the deep, and secret things of Grace, and the mysteries of Christs King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom: All this is comfortable to the Saints, and glorious to God.</ns0:note>; he knoweth what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the darkness <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">He knoweth what is in darkness, and dwelleth with him, and he in it. He sees and foresees the most hidden things; <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />niel</ns0:hi> points at the Kings dream in the night, which he onely gave the King, and then took it from him, and then gave it <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> for him again.</ns0:note>, and the light dwelleth with him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 I thank thee, and praise thee, O thou God of my fathers <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Here he gives his God another distinguishing title from all the gods of the Heathen, he calls him the <ns0:hi>God of his Fathers</ns0:hi> meaning the Covenant made with <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> &c. to whom and their Seed God revealed his saving knowledge, which he did not to the Heathen. God is the God of all by the Kingdom of his power, but the God of his church, only according to the Kingdom of his grace.</ns0:note>, who hast given me wisdom and might, and hast made known unto me now what we desired of thee: for thou hast <ns0:hi>now</ns0:hi> made known unto us the kings matter <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">In which words he intimates a twofold priviledge<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the one that as the Son of such Fathers, he obtained the grace and favour of God in giving him safety and wisdom; the other
that he found him a God hearing Prayer, and that in a thing of a high nature, he <ns0:hi>made known to him the Kings matter.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:132" />24 ¶ Therefore Daniel wen<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> in unto Arioch <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Being now prepared he goes to <ns0:hi>Arioch</ns0:hi> to go in with him to the King.</ns0:note> whom the king had ordained to destroy the wise <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> of Babylon; he went and said thus unto him, Destroy not the wise <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He bid him stay his hand<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and not destroy the wise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />men of <ns0:hi>Babylon. Arioch</ns0:hi> might plead the Kings Command, <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> tells him that was because they could not tell the Kings dream: come saith he I will shew that, by that I take away the ground of thy Commission to destroy. <ns0:hi>Qu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t.</ns0:hi> Did <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> do well in de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />siring to have them spared, who deserved to dye for their un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lawful Arts, Diviners, Necromancers, &c. <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Two things are usually answered to this. 1. They were not all such, some were innocent, studied arts and Sciences lawful and laudable. 2. Those that were otherwise, he pleaded not for them as such, but for justice, that they ought not to dye unjustly: and that was their case and cause.</ns0:note> of Babylon, bring me before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Then Arioch brought in Daniel before the king in hast, and said thus unto him, <ns0:note place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>that I <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 span">
                           <ns0:desc>〈…〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> I have found a man <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">How comes <ns0:hi>Arioch</ns0:hi> to boast of what he had found; as if he got him by great search, or by great chance, and as if <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> had been some obscure unknown person, when <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> had asked time of the King just before. It is the manner of Courtiers to be very officious, and to commend their own little deeds, that thereby they may signifie something with their Prince, and make themselves necessary to him, but possibly <ns0:hi>Arioch</ns0:hi> might not know that <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> had been with the King, and therefore comes with this (<ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>) I have found your man, here he is, behold him, he will give the King full satisfaction in all, concerning the Dream.</ns0:note> of the <ns0:note place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of the cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ty of Iudah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> captives of Judah, that will make known unto the king the interpreta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 The king answered and said to Daniel, whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Belteshazzar <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">By this name of <ns0:hi>Belteshazzar</ns0:hi> he had given <ns0:hi>Daniel,</ns0:hi> he took courage as if he might expect some great thing from him: for the word signifies the keeper of secret treasure, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to lay up and bring forth.</ns0:note>, Art thou able to make known unto me the dream which I have seen, and the interpretation thereof <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As if he had said I question if thou canst seeing all my wise men cannot do it, canst thou presume to do more then all they.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded, cannot the wise <ns0:hi>men,</ns0:hi> the astrologers, the magicians, the sooth-sayers shew unto the king, <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">He reckons up here all sorts of divination, to shew that di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vine things, and the secrets of God, cannot be comprehended by man without special Revelation; and that those who pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sume to do it arrogate too much to themselves, and that it is too Tyrannical to require it of any, and that upon pain of death; for saith <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> they cannot do it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 But there is a God in heaven that reveal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth secrets <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Hereby the Prophet gives God intirely all the glory, pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving all the powers on Earth to come short in it, it being one of Gods peculiar Prerogatives to reveal secrets. Yea in great humility he denies himself to have any share in it, as also <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 29.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hald. <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ath <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> known.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar, what shall be in the latter days <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Observe here the Prophets wisdom in this discove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, he doth not fall abruptly upon the dream, but first prepares this lofty King for it in general, and by degrees, he doth labour to win him to the knowledge of the true God, 1. By this his power. And 2. By his gracious favour to the King, in reveal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to him the greatest secret in the World about the change of Kingdoms and Governments, and touching the power of Christs Kingdom over all in the latter dayes. See <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 44.</ns0:note>. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 <ns0:hi>As for</ns0:hi> thee, O king, thy thoughts <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hald. <ns0:hi>came</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> came into <ns0:hi>thy mind,</ns0:hi> upon thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter; and he that revealeth secrets maketh known unto thee what shall come to pass.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>en. 41.16.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>3.12.</ns0:note> But <ns0:hi>as for</ns0:hi> me, this secret is not revealed to me, for <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> wisdom that I have more than any living, but <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>that they <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ight make known,</ns0:hi> So Gr.</ns0:note> for <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> sakes that shall make known the interpretation to the king <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Some will have this relate to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> and the Church of God, by whose Prayers this was obtained<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but the more plain sense is this, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> that the interpretation may be manifest to the King<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and that thou maist know the thoughts of thy heart, that thou maist be better instructed and satisfied in thy mind in this great secret, when thou seest the mind of God in it, and what it points <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, and wha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> thy duty is, and how to steer thy coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel and a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tions in this vast Monarchy, and towards the afflicted Church of God in it.</ns0:note>, and that thou mightest know the thoughts of thy heart.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 Thou, O king, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>wast seeing.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sawest, and behold, a great image <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Not a painted superficial image, but a massy one<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> a Statue in mans shape, great, splendid, majestical, thus they were wont to represent of old, great Emperors, and Empires, and worshipped them as gods, called here an Image, and in a dream all which is in shew, and shadow rather then in substance, and therefore vanishing. And that upright, of a prodigious height, noting the grand<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ur of those Monarchies.</ns0:note>: this great image whose bright<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> excellent, stood before thee <ns0:hi>b,</ns0:hi> and the form thereof <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> terrible <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Government is to be feared<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ar to whom fear, a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>d <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>our to whom ho<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>r,</ns0:hi> also some had rather be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ared then loved. Some say the Image was so po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ited, that the face looked toward the King, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hus it might trouble and terrifie him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 This images head <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> of fine gold, his breast and his arms of silver, his belly and his <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>sides.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> thighs of brass.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 His legs of iron, his feet part of iron and part of clay <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">By this we see the World is much worse and far declined, every age degenerating from what it was of old<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as the Poets which borrowed their fancy from this Image, have described the ages of the World from Mettals, the first was golden, and so coming on courser, it ended at last as this Image in the Text in dirt.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 Thou sawest till that a stone was cut out <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>not in <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ands, as ver.</ns0:hi> 45.</ns0:note>
without hands, which smote the image upon his feet <ns0:hi>that were</ns0:hi> of iron and clay, and broke them to pieces <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All of it to pieces, all vanished, <ns0:hi>and the Stone became a great M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nt and filled the whole Earth,</ns0:hi> this is the dream; and the interpretation of all follows.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver and the gold broken to pieces together, and became <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Hos. 13.3.</ns0:note> like the chaff of the summers threshing floors, and the winds carried them away, that no place was found for them: and
the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the dream, and we will tell the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpretation thereof, before the king <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By this word <ns0:hi>we</ns0:hi> appears <ns0:hi>Daniels</ns0:hi> Piety and Modesty, for he declares by it, that he and his Companions had begged this skill from God, and therefore he did not, nor could arrogate it to himself excluding them, without injury; and dishonour to God that heard Prayer. Now begins the interpretation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 Thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezra 7.12. Jer. 27.6, 7. Ezek. 26.7. Hos. 8.10.</ns0:note>, O king, <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> a king of kings <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He means <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> in person together with his Suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessors, <ns0:hi>Evilmerodac,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bel<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>hazzar</ns0:hi> the Prophet would not mind the King of any thing past, nor of any other Governments but those with whom his Church were then and to be concern<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed for the future, till the coming of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> by whose com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing they should support and comfort themselves against all their sufferings by oppressors, and also God would have the Prophet mind <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> of the Stone cut out of the Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain without hands, growing and breaking in pieces all earthly power.</ns0:note>, for the God of heaven hath given thee a <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>the kingdom, the power,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">It came not to thee by thy Ancestors or by fortune, or by thy valour, but the great God of Heaven hath the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stowing of those, and giveth them to whomsoever he will.</ns0:note>, power, and strength, and glory <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Au<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thority; victorious Armies, with great prosperity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 And wheresoever the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field and the fowls of the heaven hath he given into thine hand, and hath made thee ruler over them all <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I have given thee absolute dominion of all Creatures, Men and Beasts within the bounds of thy vast Kingdom, to hunt, catch, or kill for thy use, and pleasure. God as Lord Paramount allowes thee his Vassal, and Tenant at will all this. This was not Universal overall the World, but only within his large Territories, which yet were bounded.</ns0:note>; thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> this head of gold <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">1 Why <ns0:hi>head?</ns0:hi> Because he was first in order, as the head is before the other parts, and the vision began in him, and descended downwards to the other three Monarchies. 2. <ns0:hi>Why head of Gold?</ns0:hi> Because of the vast riches wherein it abounded, and which the <ns0:hi>Chalde<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ans</ns0:hi> most coveted, and scraped from the spoiles and tributes of all Countries, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 10<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>13, 14. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 51.41, 44. Also this is cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led the golden head, because it stood longest, 500 years, and was fortunate and flourishing to the last.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:133" />39 And after thee shall arise another kingdom inferiour to thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This was that of the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians,</ns0:hi> inferiour in time and succession, in duration it lasted not half so long, as the <ns0:hi>As<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />syrian</ns0:hi> in prosperity and tranquility, for the <ns0:hi>Persian</ns0:hi> was fuller of trouble; yet was this wonderful rich and large for a time, <ns0:hi>Esther</ns0:hi> 1.1. this was the Breast and Armes of Silver.</ns0:note>, and another third kingdom of brass <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This was the <ns0:hi>Graecian</ns0:hi> Monarchy, under <ns0:hi>Alexander</ns0:hi> the great, who conquered the former, called the <ns0:hi>City</ns0:hi> because given so much to Luxury; <ns0:hi>Brass,</ns0:hi> because courser then the other, and their Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mou<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> was chiefly Brass, <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>, which shall bear rule over all the earth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Therefore this is also called an universal Monarchy; for <ns0:hi>Alexander</ns0:hi> marched into the <ns0:hi>Indies,</ns0:hi> and conquered much of that, by which he was said to conquer the World; and wept that he had not another World to conquer, yet this lasted not long for he was soon over<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />come, and kild by his worldly lusts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 And the fourth Kingdom shall be strong as iron: forasmuch as iron breaketh in pieces, and subdueth all <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This is the Kingdom of the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi>; and was to last not only to <ns0:hi>Christs</ns0:hi> first coming, but under <ns0:hi>Antichrist,</ns0:hi> to his second coming, but still going down as to Pagan Worship<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and at last to Antichristian and Papal power; for <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 28. <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> tells the King, that God made known to him what should be in the lat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter dayes; therefore he intended a general History to the end of the World, <ns0:hi>verse</ns0:hi> 44. and <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 7. latter end<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 11. and 12.</ns0:note>: and as iron that breaketh all these, shall it break in pieces and bruise <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This did break in pieces all other Kingdoms, being too strong for them, and was never in subjection to any, but brought all in subjection to it, till the stone fell upon it, of which afterward.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">41 And whereas thou sawest the feet and toes, part of potters clay, and part of iron: the kingdom shall be divided <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Partly strong and partly weak; The <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> Kingdom was divided, partly because <ns0:hi>Tyranny</ns0:hi> followed <ns0:hi>Aristocracy,</ns0:hi> and the Government made up of both, partly their Civil Wars, when two Competitors s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>rove each for dominion, the common peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple against the Senate, <ns0:hi>Sylla</ns0:hi> against <ns0:hi>Marius, Caesar</ns0:hi> against <ns0:hi>Pom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pey,</ns0:hi> also, partly when conquered Provinces and Kingdoms cast off the <ns0:hi>Roman</ns0:hi> yoke, and set up Kings of their own<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and so the Empire was divided into ten Kingdoms or Toes. The vision attributes two legs to the Image, and to the fourth <ns0:hi>Monarchy,</ns0:hi> because the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> had sometimes <ns0:hi>duumvirs,</ns0:hi> two <ns0:hi>Consuls,</ns0:hi> two <ns0:hi>Emperors,</ns0:hi> one in the East, the other in the West.</ns0:note>, but there shall be in it of the strength of the iron, forasmuch as thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 And <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the toes of the feet <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> part of iron, and part of clay; <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>brittle.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> broken <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This was plain in the Civil Wars of the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> the falling off of some Countries, especially in and towards the end of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 And whereas thou sawest iron mixt with miry clay, they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> By Marriage, but they shall never sodder well together, because ambition is of stronger force, then affinity and consa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                  </ns0:note> one to another, even as iron is not mixed with clay.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 And in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>their dayes.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 4.3.34. and 6.26. and 7.14, 27. Mic. 4.7. Luc. 1.33.</ns0:note> which shall never be destroyed <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> While the Iron Kingdom stood, for <ns0:hi>Christ</ns0:hi> was born in the Reign of <ns0:hi>Augustus Caesar,</ns0:hi> Luc. 2.1. <ns0:hi>Shall the God of Heaven set up a Kingdom.</ns0:hi> Now see the difference of Christs Kingdom from all other Kingdoms in the World. 1. In the rise of it, it was not by earthly succession, or armes, or policy. 2. It is Spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual and Heavenly in the Lawes and Administration of it. 3. Jesus Christ was not a meer Man, but God-Man, he is the King, the Son of God. 4<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> It is stronger then all other, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it breaks them in pieces. 5. It is not bounded by any li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mits as Worldly Empires are, but truly Universal. 6 It shall be for ever, and never<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> destroyed and given to others, as the rest were.</ns0:note>, and the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom thereof.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> kingdom shall not be left to other people, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> it shall break in pieces, and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> without hands, and that it brake in pieces the iron, the brass, the clay, the silver and the gold <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">1. This notes the small beginning of Christ Kingdom vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sibly. 2. The different rise of Christs from all other; His Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ception by the Holy Ghost, like as <ns0:hi>Melchizedeck,</ns0:hi> without Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther and Mother, respectively as to his two Natures; <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 9.6. who shall declare his Generation; his name shall be called wonderful. 3. This stone as a heavy Rock, tumbling down from the Mountain, brake the image in pieces, which could not be said any other did so. 4. Christ is a stone that grinds to powder those it falls on. He is the pretious foundation and chief corner stone of his Church for ever. 5. He is a growing stone even to a Mountain, and therefore will fill the Earth, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.24.</ns0:note>, the great God hath made known to the king what shall come to pass <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Chald. <ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap> this.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> hereafter <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The great God hath shewn all this, who is above all the Kings of the Earth, and only knows, and decrees, and effects future things, who only doth great and wondrous things.</ns0:note>: and the dream <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> certain <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> This dream is no ordinary dream, but an Oracle of God; it is sent from Heaven, and gives a perfect scheme and Prophetical Hi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />story of things to come, about the special Providence of God, in changing Governors and Governments, with particular re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard to his Church under them, and above all, about the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of Christ, and the growth of it, maugre all the enter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prizes of Pagan and Antichristian <ns0:hi>Rome.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and the interpretation thereof sure <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">It is not a conjec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tural guess of the <ns0:hi>Magicians,</ns0:hi> and wise men of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> who use to prepare lying words, because they have no knowledge of the true God, and therefore are wholly unacquainted with his secrets, which he revealeth to his Prophets by the Spirit of Prophesie, which he hath now signally imparted to me, which I have faithfully made known unto thee O King.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> worshipped Daniel, and command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed that they should offer an oblation, and sweet odours unto him <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This was strange, that so great a Monarch should thus wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship his Vassal; thus was it sometimes done to men, as to <ns0:hi>Elias</ns0:hi> the Prophet, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 1.13. this was done in consternation and admiration, because he saw so much of God in the Prophet, and in the revelation of the dream; but why did <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> suffer it to be done to him? 1. Though he could not hinder the King in his prostration, and in his word of command, yet doubtless he shewed his averseness with much zeal and abhor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence, as the <ns0:hi>Apostles</ns0:hi> did in the like case, <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 14.13, 14, 15. because it was high Sacriledge and Idolatry. 2 It is not said they offered Sacrifice to <ns0:hi>Daniel,</ns0:hi> but only the King commanded it, which doubtless <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> refused, because he was so careful in not defiling himself with the Kings dainties, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.8. also, when he would not omit the Worship of God, though with the hazard of his Life, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.10. therefore the King being in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structed of <ns0:hi>Daniel,</ns0:hi> gives God all the glory, in the next words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="47">47 The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth <ns0:hi>it is,</ns0:hi> that your God is a God of gods <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">A God of Gods, the greatest and supream God of all the World, above <ns0:hi>Baal,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Bel,</ns0:hi> and above all other gods.</ns0:note>, and a Lord of kings <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The word is <ns0:hi>maron</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>maran,</ns0:hi> which in the <ns0:hi>Syriac</ns0:hi> signifies <ns0:hi>Lord,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>high Lord,</ns0:hi> seeing he is the highest King of all the earth. He makes, over-rules, and pulls down whom he will, 1 <ns0:hi>T<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>m.</ns0:hi> 6.15. <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 17.14. and 19.16. by this he gathers, that God is a <ns0:hi>re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vealer of secrets, Isa.</ns0:hi> 48.3, 5, 6, 7, 8.</ns0:note>, and a revealer of secrets <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Is supream God, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he knowes, and foreknowes, and decrees all things fu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture.</ns0:note>, seeing thou couldest reveal this se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cret <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Therefore <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> had it from God, who revealed it to him, which here the King confesseth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="48">48 Then the king made Daniel a great man <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Chald. <ns0:hi>Rabbi</ns0:hi> magnified him.</ns0:note>, and gave him many great gifts <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">An estate suitable to his honour.</ns0:note>, and made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Gnal col medina</ns0:hi> over the chief Province of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> which was head, because of the Metropolis, the word is also <ns0:hi>Arabick,</ns0:hi> and therefore used in <ns0:hi>Spain</ns0:hi> at this day.</ns0:note>, and chief of the governors over all the wise <ns0:hi>men</ns0:hi> of Babylon <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 4.9. <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> was chief of them in wisdom, for he could unfold what none of the wise men could. Again, he was chief in place and power, he had the rule, and inspection of them, which were students and professors of wisdom and learning, into their stu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dies and manners, like a perpetual Lord Chancellour, not that this Holy Prophet gave any incouragement to them in their un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lawful arts and divinations, but rather discouraged and correct<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them, teaching them the knowledge of the true God: thus doth the true Religion top all the World, and make the gran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deur thereof stoop to it, for it is the wisdom of God, and the power of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="49">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:133" />49 Then Daniel requested of the king, and he set Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego over the affairs of the province of Babylon: but Daniel <ns0:hi>sat</ns0:hi> in the gate of the king <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He substituted them as Lieutenants for the Kings service, under <ns0:hi>Daniel,</ns0:hi> which as the curious observe, was chiefly about agriculture, and gathering revenues and provisions for the Court, but <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> he was as Privy Counsellour and Lord Chamberlain, about arduous affairs of the King and Kingdom, sitting some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times in judgment, and also admitting and conducting persons and causes to the King, as there was need, to whom there was difficult access, according to the Magnificence and Majesty of the Kings of the East. Thus <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> sate in the Kings Gate, to be near and ready for the Kings chiefest business, and it notes honour, also high favour, but especiallly we must look upon <ns0:hi>Daniels</ns0:hi> promotion to be for the service and protection of his brethren in their present state of Captivity, as <ns0:hi>Mordecai</ns0:hi> was, which shewes that God doth remember his people in their low estate, and doth not leave himself without witness to them, in raising up nursing fathers for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Poole.heading: CHAP. II. In this Chapter are four principal parts. 1. The Kings Dream, ver. 1.2. The wisemens Ignorance and Danger, to ver. 14. 3. The Revelation and Interpretation of the Dream by Daniel, to ver. 48.4. The advancement of Daniel to great Honour by that means, ver. 48.49.
